When Alexandru Voica, head of corporate affairs at the video-generation startup Synthesia, sent me a link this summer to the newest addition to their PR team, I was surprised. It was an interactive virtual avatar of him, trained to answer common press questions about Synthesia, like what it does and how it works. highlights.title: Man City chairman responds to reports surrounding 115 charges
highlights.summary: Manchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak has reaffirmed his belief the club will prove their innocence in the Premier League 115 charges case following reports on Friday.
body: Sky Sports News understands that the process is moving to the appeal stage, after reports claimed that most of the charges against the club for breaking Financial Fair Play rules were found to have been proven.
However, in a statement released on Saturday afternoon, the City chairman said "our confidence and intent in proving the club's innocence is just as strong as when this began."

Describing his stance on the situation, Al Mubarak said in a message to City's supporters: "Following Friday's media reporting, many of you will have spent your evening answering questions and responding to messages from friends, family and colleagues. So have I. Here's what I said to my family: The Premier League process still has a long way to run, and our confidence and intent in proving the club's innocence is just as strong as when this began.

"There are so many things that I would like to be able to share with you to help you understand why we feel so confident in our position. But the strict confidentiality of the legal process and our determination to respect it means I cannot do that at the moment. Even this letter underwent several legal checks to make sure it complies."

highlights.title: 26 years ago, 'Buffy the Vampire Slayer's Worst Season Premiere Redefined a Legendary Villain
highlights.summary: Ever since, Dracula has evolved into an enduring figure, often treated as the final boss in most vampiric tier lists. Dracula has appeared in everything from Nosferatu (1922) to Blade (1998). He typically symbolizes a grand threat that must be defeated before it's too late.
body: Vampires in fiction can be traced back to the 18th century, but these undead stock villains only became a fleshed-out archetype in Bram Stoker’s 1897 gothic horror, Dracula. In Stoker’s book, the Count is a layered metaphor for social taboos and pestilence, while his move from Transylvania to England presents themes of xenophobia.

The season 5 premiere of Buffy the Vampire Slayer, however, doesn’t treat Dracula with such reverence. Titled “ Buffy vs. Dracula,” the episode features Buffy Summers (Sarah Michelle Gellar) being confronted by Count Dracula (Rudolf Martin), who unceremoniously appears in Sunnydale to seek out the renowned Slayer.

“Get out!” Buffy retorts with skepticism after her first meeting with the Count, initially dismissing him as a “fanboy” like the countless vampires who “call themselves Lestat.” The rest is an expectedly campy showdown between the Slayer and the Count, turning “Buffy vs. Dracula” into a fun, albeit lackluster season premiere.

highlights.title: MIT students gain a humanist lens on technical innovation in Tulsa, Oklahoma
highlights.summary: The PKG Center expands Code.Tulsa, an internship program that places MIT students with tribal nations and Tulsa nonprofits to develop AI and data science projects while gaining humanistic perspectives on technology's role in community development.
body: When MIT mechanical engineering student Daphne Wang arrived for her internship at the Muscogee Creek Nation Department of Health in Tulsa, Oklahoma last summer, she expected to be writing code. To her surprise, she found herself analyzing tribal history and the implications for technical innovation.

“I learned so much that I think should be required curriculum for every single person in this country,” says Wang. “I think tech for good is genuinely getting out into communities and learning about people who aren't you, creating worldly perspectives that you ultimately can take into everything else that you do.”

Wang and fellow intern Lucy Sun, who is majoring in artificial intelligence and decision making, spent the summer supporting the development of the Muscogee Nation's first Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System (PRAMS) survey to capture maternal health data specific to Muscogee women. The project required completing literature reviews, analyzing datasets, and drafting survey questions, while considering issues of data sovereignty and governance structures specific to the Muscogee.

highlights.title: Warwickshire win County Championship
highlights.summary: Warwickshire thrashed visitors Leicestershire by an innings and 79 runs at Edgbaston to seal a ninth County Championship title and their first since 2021 on Saturday.
body: They entered the third day needing seven wickets to clinch the title, while the visitors needed 182 more runs to send them back in to bat.

Chris Woakes got the hosts off to the ideal start by bowling Sol Budinger for 47 and the former England all-rounder soon struck again when his delivery to Jonathan Tattersall was caught by Rob Yates at slip.

Leicestershire began to crumble as Ethan Bamber claimed the scalps of Ben Cox and Ben Green in quick succession and skipper Ian Holland was trapped lbw by Ed Barnard as the hosts closed in on the title.
Ajaz Patel was bowled by Manav Suthar, but Leicestershire dug in with a productive final-wicket partnership between Tom Scriven and Josh Hull.

highlights.title: ‘I was mesmerised by how the fog turned the tower into a monolith’: Derek Zhao’s best phone picture
highlights.summary: Zhao was out jogging around Treasure Island, near San Francisco, when he spotted a lonely tower stabbing through the clouds. Every morning, Derek Zhao jogs the perimeter of Treasure Island, his home, situated an eight-minute ferry ride from San Francisco.
body: Zhao works as a machine-learning engineer at Disney California. He relocated from Texas last year to take up the role, finding the 400-acre human-made island to be the perfect location, “close enough to the office and all the culture the city has to offer, but far enough that I’m waking up to the sound of seagulls instead of car horns”.

He took this image earlier this year, stopping mid-jog to capture the top of San Francisco’s Salesforce Tower. “I was mesmerised by how the fog, caused by what’s known as a marine layer, completely covered the rest of the skyline, leaving only the tower looking like a monolith,” he says. “It’s ironic that something that obscures, like fog, can make a scene more clear.”

It’s only recently that Zhao has come to realise that his favourite photos don’t come from travels with his professional cameras, but “improbable scenes near home that somehow only reveal themselves when I’m not expecting them. It brings me considerable peace that despite living in such close proximity to the centre of things I feel ambivalent about – tech, AI, urban density, hustle culture – the universe can still grant such awe-inspiring moments of quiet.

highlights.title: Can Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince save the web from AI?
highlights.summary: Today, I’m talking with Matthew Prince, who is CEO of Cloudflare. This episode is part of a two-part series on the future of business. Matthew last joined us on the show about two and a half years ago, at what we thought then was a wild pivot point for the internet — and now it
body: Cloudflare found in June that bots made up more than half of internet traffic. That number just keeps going up as more and more AI companies scrape more and more of the web, and now as more and more AI agents try and do things for people on the web. Cloudflare sits between websites and all those agents, and allows website owners some level of control: Owners can block all those AI tools, allow them, or, as you’ll hear, only allow those that might pay money for access.

So Matthew and I talked about how to control all these bots, what kind of mess they’re making of the web, and what kinds of information might be valuable in the future as some of the payment schemes come into focus. You’ll hear me ask pretty directly if some of the outcomes he’s describing are actually good — Matthew is a thoughtful guy, and his answer is something I’m still thinking about well after we had this conversation.

highlights.title: Magic: The Gathering Meets D&D-Style Dice Battles in the Best New TCG at PAX West 2026
highlights.summary: 2026 has been, in several crucial ways, an HD remake of the late '90s and early 2000s. My old boot-cut jeans are inexplicably back in fashion, live-action Spider-Man and Resident Evil movies are hitting theaters, no one will shut up about Wolverine, and the last nerd convention I went to hosted a…
body: At PAX West in Seattle, most of that battle unfolded inside Summit, the newer of the Washington State Convention Center's two buildings. Its tabletop floor featured official booths for Riftbound, OverPower, Rush of Ikorr, and the Gundam Card Game. In previous years, it had struck me that Magic: The Gathering had more or less taken over the TCG space, at least at PAX. Now there are multiple contenders visibly gunning for its throne.

One of the more interesting challengers, however, was hiding a few blocks away. The World of Kylia booth was half-hidden in the Arch building's expo hall. Here, the local Washington company iQ Pictures was showing off their card game Ascendant, which just celebrated its second anniversary.

According to its creator, Chase Lambert-Crittenden, the world of Kylia as a whole began as a side project while he was working towards an animation degree in California. Kylia is an inhabitable world in a distant galaxy, which naturally produces a valuable plasma-like substance called Genki. In the present day, Kylia is home to multiple native and alien species, who exist alongside one another in seven separate nations.

highlights.title: Control Resonant is a great game — it’s even better when you read everything
highlights.summary: In Control Resonant, the entire world is at stake. But that didn't stop the diligent employees of the Federal Bureau of Control from filing reams of paperwork, and it didn't stop me from reading everything I could find, either.
body: There’s a lot to read in Remedy’s Control sequel, even just in the menus. It’s worth taking the time to pore over it all.

In the world of Control Resonant and its predecessor, 2019’s Control, the FBC deals with mysterious, otherworldly objects and entities that defy explanation. But the FBC itself is still an old-school bureaucratic agency, and that means tons of (often heavily redacted) reports and memos and miscellaneous bits of paper to sort through. I like reading, and I especially like reading Remedy’s clever and often funny writing, but I was overwhelmed at first by the sheer amount of text.

Initially I skipped documents that seemed optional: the enemy logs, which are compiled in a separate tab and unlocked automatically after fighting each enemy type for the first time. I was kind of busy just learning how to get around — I’m not the best at spatial reasoning in general, and gravity doesn’t always matter in Resonant ’s M.C. Escher-ified version of Manhattan. I was also too busy beating down the game’s many Hiss and mold enemies to read about them.

But that didn't stop the diligent employees of the Federal Bureau of Control from filing reams of paperwork, and it didn't stop me from reading everything I could find, either.

highlights.title: Proaction boosts sales 60% and saves 75+ hours with Codex
highlights.summary: With Codex, GPT-Live-1, and GPT-6 Astra, Proaction builds, operates, and sells modern fleet management faster.
body: Proaction ⁠ (opens in a new window) builds software for businesses that manage fleets of vehicles, from cars and trucks to construction machinery. Because every fleet operates differently, showing prospects how Proaction’s platform fits their business is an essential part of selling it.
But personalized demos required engineering time the team couldn’t spare. The founders had to rely on conversations and slide decks to explain what was possible. Codex flipped the script.

“As a non-technical person, I used to have to loop engineers in if I wanted a demo,” says Colin Knudsen, co-founder and COO of Proaction. “Now I do it myself in Codex.” Colin creates four to six customized, interactive demos a month, with each taking 30 to 45 minutes to build. He estimates that this avoids 40 to 60 hours of engineering work.

After a sales call, Colin directs Codex to the Granola recording, prospect email threads, and any spreadsheets the prospect has shared. Codex uses that context to customize an HTML demo environment that mirrors Proaction’s product and the customer’s own fleet.
points: With Codex, GPT-Live-1, and GPT-6 Astra, Proaction builds, operates, and sells modern fleet management faster.

highlights.title: Control Resonant Violates the Number One Commandment of Video Game Lore
highlights.summary: So much of Control, Remedy Entertainment’s 2019 paranatural shooter, sticks with me today, but the one thing I really remember is its lore. Its setting, a Brutalist Manhattan office building called The Oldest House, is littered with paperwork covered in black redactions, so much of which explains…
body: It makes sense, then, that Remedy would double down on what it did best for Control Resonant. Though the sequel takes the series out of The Oldest House and onto the Hiss-infected streets of Manhattan, protagonist Dylan Faden still stumbles upon plenty of notes and audio logs left behind in an apocalyptic event. But what should be a selling point for Resonant is one of its minor pain points: There’s just too much lore to sift through.

That’s not a knock against the quality of Remedy’s writing, mind you; every piece of lore I’ve found in Resonant so far is top-notch. Something as simple as a tuning fork puzzle in a subway gets elevated by notes that paint a picture of a frustrated research team trying to understand why they keep teleporting around. It makes every piece of Resonant ’s world feel narratively motivated rather than something that’s there for the sake of gameplay. That’s what puts Remedy head and shoulders above so many of its peers as a big-budget developer.

highlights.summary: The former child star — famous for telling Tom Cruise "a human head weighs eight pounds" in 'Jerry Maguire' — opens up about baring all in the Lance Oppenheim-directed film, being brave and staying stubborn for what he loves most: "I don't quit."
body: A little more than a year ago, Jonathan Lipnicki started praying nightly for clarity in his career.

It worked. Not long after, Lipnicki arrived at a new gig, and while it didn’t deliver the most amount of screen time in his lengthy IMDb credits, it delivered the boldest turn of the 35-year-old’s career. Lipnicki — a beloved child star who, at age 6, hit the jackpot by making his debut opposite Tom Cruise and Renée Zellweger in Cameron Crowe’s Jerry Maguire before moving on to other hits like Stuart Little — snagged a part in Lance Oppenheim ‘s Primetime for A24.

That applies to Lipnicki, who shed more than that — specifically, his pants — for a full frontal scene complete with a can of whipped cream. “As actors, we pray for dark material and for things we can really sink our teeth into. At the end of the day, you have to ask yourself, ‘Am I as courageous an artist as I say I am?’ I had to answer that question, and I was courageous enough to take the plunge,” Lipnicki told The Hollywood Reporter over Zoom in September. “I’ve tried to live by the idea that, when it comes to art, if something scares you, most likely you should do it.”

highlights.title: How Athens discovered a new, confident Greek cuisine
highlights.summary: Athens is now a food capital where you can enjoy bustling bars, traditional taverna fare or unearth a new-wave gem in its many restaurants – but it wasn’t always this way See our recommendations for eating and drinking around Athens.
body: Visiting Athens for its food might have sounded like a joke to previous generations. Unlike many other Mediterranean countries, including Italy, Spain and Turkey, Greece had no renaissance and no aristocracy to fund chefs and develop sophisticated cuisines. Simple village dishes didn’t always translate well: in the past, tourists would suffer a summer scorching and some desiccated moussaka so they could puff up the Acropolis in August before skedaddling to an island. However, recently the Greek capital has undergone a gastronomic renaissance.

In the 1980s, Athenians were leaving behind a history of rural poverty, fasoláda bean stew, and a largely vegetarian diet. They discovered fast food and began eating too much meat. The 1990s saw new levels of wealth; brunch, sushi and lobster spaghetti were aspirational goals for the upwardly mobile. By the time of the 2004 Athens Olympics, a cohort of Athenians existed who had never known hunger, war or dictatorship. Consequently, the economic crisis that began in 2009 was a devastating shock and the next decade saw severe unemployment and deprivation, accompanied by an influx of traumatised refugees and migrants.

highlights.title: Old-School Credit Card Scams Are Far From Dead
highlights.summary: In an era of increasingly sophisticated AI-fueled scams, a retro threat may be lurking in your mailbox.
body: When every random text message feels like it’s a scam, and with AI supercharging digital fraud, old-time credit card skimmers and bogus letters that arrive in the mail may seem laughable as potential threats in 2026. But as we all suffer through a seemingly unending barrage of potential scams, these antiquated attacks are still costing victims around the world dearly.

If someone scans the QR code, they’re typically redirected to a fake banking website, where they’re asked to enter their details—potentially giving cybercriminals direct access to their real accounts. “This has been escalating for close to two years, and I believe that this type of scam might have proven to be successful enough to be rolled out in other countries,” Hauer says. “The cost of producing a personalized fake card has dropped in recent years thanks to AI just being able to copy a design based on an image, and the higher conversion rate per victim might justify the extra costs.”

body: Anthropic lost a legal battle to overturn one of the supply-chain risk labels that the US Department of Defense slapped on the company, as a federal appeals court in DC on Friday refused to second-guess the Trump administration.

“The department had ample support for its conclusion that the continued integration of Claude into the department’s information systems, by the department or its contractors, presented a statutorily covered national-security risk,” the judges wrote in a majority opinion. “As Anthropic admits, the company encodes restrictions into Claude that prevent the model from performing tasks that Anthropic wishes to prevent.”

Anthropic spokesperson Danielle Cohen says the company remains confident in its position and is considering all options. That could include appealing to a broader panel of the DC Circuit Court of Appeals or the US Supreme Court.

highlights.title: Cooking with Tom Kerridge, the Michelin ‘meatfluencer’
highlights.summary: The star chef demystified the restaurant scene with his love of a welcoming pub. Now he explains why hospitality is in crisis – and how to make a sublime venison chilli.
body: Tom Kerridge is the king of meat: first as a chef, transforming pub classics like pork belly into Michelin-starred fare at The Hand and Flowers in Marlow 20 years ago, and later opening The Butcher’s Tap and Grill in the same village; then as a cookery writer: his Outdoor Cooking – The Ultimate Modern Barbecue Bible of 2021 is well named, being both as comprehensive and as worshipful as a holy book; and recently as a “meat-fluencer”, making gorgeous skills videos on Instagram and YouTube.

That was just destiny, he says (more or less). “When you’re cooking in a classic brigade system, the sections are like a larder: you’ve got starters, you’ve got garnish, you’ve got meat and fish, you’ve got pastry. The meat is the lead section, where the most experienced chef is, because that’s where you land when you’ve learned to treat vegetables with love and respect. If you fuck up cabbage, it doesn’t cost a lot.” It’s true, it doesn’t, but if you saw the care Kerridge puts into dicing an onion – peeling its layers apart like he’s making a mosaic, assiduous even about half an inch of waste – of an onion – you’d know that love and respect aren’t really about money.
